verdict.tagline: Grand strategy burdened by steep learning curves and expansion costs.
for_you_if: you enjoy complex historical simulation games
you can invest time into learning intricate mechanics
you embrace extensive community modding support
not_for_you_if: you want a complete experience without purchasing multiple expansions
you cannot tolerate startup failures and random crashes
you dislike navigating nested menus for basic actions

cohorts.label: 2-20h
cohorts.summary: Early players navigate complex nested menus and steep learning curves alongside reported crashes.

claims.claim: The user interface relies heavily on nested menus, sub-menus, and tooltips that require navigating a maze to find specific actions.

citations.review_text:
Massively split on my experience so far. It's a fantastic game with... Issues.

Many hours into a campaign and whilst travelling as an adventurer for a quest I overwrite my save. I then find out there's a 'Travel Bug' with adventurer characters where upon completing a contract, they're forever stuck 'travelling' and no actions work. Completely thrown my entire campaign.

There's also a bunch of content that appears (but may not be) AI generated. The frequent use of em dashs and oddly worded text feels very 'Claudified', especially when the text doesn't make coherent sense, which could just be human error. I'll try to update with examples at some point. (Again, might not be AI, but there's plenty of textual issues.)

The UI is also atrocious for newcomers, with SO MUCH content hidden away in mini menus (often feeling like a bunch of randomly stapled on features or functions) that you'll likely have a browser tab open in the background to search for 'How Tos' constantly in your first few hours.

That all said, this is so addictive. The concept, the experience, the highs and lows are all thoroughly enjoyable.

A mostly fantastic game, but a bug like this for the adventurer (that appears to have been around for a while according to forums) and the 'AI-ified content' completely kills the game and experience for me.

There are so many menus, sub-menus, 'helpful' pop-ups and tooltips that I'm forced to click through a maze to find the thing that lets me do what I want to do. And then, once I find it, the game's mechanics and terms around diplomatically managing titles and holdings are impossible to figure out unless you have a degree in history. I shouldn't have to watch YouTube tutorials and read wiki guides to understand how your game works - that's just bad design. I'm sure there's a rich, engaging strategy simulation waiting behind the barrier for entry but the early-game experience is a turn-off. I don't mind a game making me feel dumb and powerless so long as it's entertaining, but this is a chore. I regret giving this game the benefit of the doubt through a 2nd and 3rd try because I'm likely ineligible for a refund due to playtime hours logged.

Ah yes, and F partition succession!

The game itself is well made, with solid strategic depth, excellent replayability, and enough variety to make every playthrough feel different.

Unfortunately, Paradox's DLC policy completely undermines the experience. The base game feels intentionally stripped down, to the point where it's hard to recommend playing it without buying multiple expansions. To get what I would consider a complete and enjoyable experience, you realistically need at least 3–4 DLCs, whose combined cost exceeds the price of the base game.

That's simply not fair to players who already paid for the game. A €30 DLC should significantly expand an already complete experience—not sell back features that feel essential. Instead, the vanilla version often feels incomplete, while the DLCs are treated as mandatory purchases rather than optional expansions.

I don't mind paying for quality content, but Paradox's approach makes it feel like the real game is locked behind a very expensive paywall. It's a disappointing business model for an otherwise excellent game.

Easily one of my favorite games of all time. You get to set your own goals and can do almost anything in the medieval world. Only complaint is that DLC content changes the game quite a bit so you kinda need them to fully experience the game (like any Paradox game).
I like the game and all but so much content blocked behind a paywall. All content probably costs over $100 + The game itself. If you got money to spare go ahead if not find a better medieval game.

cohorts.label: 100h+

claims.claim: Reviewers note that ally and enemy AI behave poorly during wars, such as allies standing idly by during sieges.

citations.review_text:
After 300+ hours in Crusader Kings III, I've realized this isn't really a strategy game. It's a medieval family disaster simulator.

You start a campaign with a simple plan. Maybe you want to unite Ireland, rebuild the Roman Empire or just create a powerful dynasty. Then 30 years later your wife is cheating on you with your brother, your heir is an alcoholic with 4 different diseases, half your kingdom has joined a faction against you, and the Pope hates you because you accidentally slept with your cousin.

And somehow it's one of the best strategy games I've ever played.

The amount of freedom CK3 gives you is insane. You can play as a tiny count with basically nothing and slowly build your family into one of the most powerful dynasties in the world. Or you can start as an emperor and watch everything your family built collapse within one generation because your character died at the worst possible time.

That's probably what makes the game so good. Losing can genuinely be more entertaining than winning.

After 300 hours I'm still discovering mechanics, events and completely ridiculous situations I've never seen before. Every campaign creates its own story, and even when I start with the exact same character, somehow everything goes completely differently.

The game definitely isn't perfect though. The AI sometimes makes decisions that make absolutely no sense, wars can be frustrating, succession will ruin your life until you understand it, and buying all the DLC isn't exactly cheap.

But once CK3 actually clicks, it's dangerously addictive.

You tell yourself you're just going to finish one war before going to bed. Then your ruler dies, so obviously you have to sort out the succession. Then your brother starts a rebellion. Then the Byzantines declare war on you. Then you notice it's 4 AM.

300+ hours and I still have absolutely no idea what I'm doing half the time.

10/10, would execute my brother for trying to steal my kingdom again.

Suggest for role playing mostly and not combat focus.  Combat mechanics are inconsistent.  Enemy and Ally AI is really bad especially for large battels (crusade, holy war).  Great potential and fun parts but poor implementation of combat.  Sad given it is medieval RP and combat sim.

The game lacks basic things like getting ur allies to join u at a siege (they almost always stay idly by while ure spending 6 months on a siege that should really take like 2 months if ur allies werent useless) and yet they keep working on useless DLCs like abbasid fashion. Like who the hell wants that?

claims.claim: Reviewers report that the learning curve is extremely steep and complex for new players.

citations.review_text: This is a pretty solid game, LOTS of options for what you can do, and what countries you can form, and how. But after a point you hit a road bump in that you've done a lot of the stuff you can do. Of course the Mod Scene is huge, and is only going to get bigger. However for newer players, even people who have played CK 2, this game's learning curve is the size of a small mountain. If you can deal with that you'll get the hang of it eventually, and hopefully have a lot of fun.
There is a learning curve and it will take time to get a hang of all the mechanics and minute details that can make or break your run BUT once that is done, there is so much you can do with the game,
Lose HOURS playing this. You have to get over the steep learning curve first.

Crusader Kings 3 is one of the most unique strategy games I’ve ever played. It stands out because it’s not just about winning wars, but about building a dynasty and telling your own story through generations.

The depth of the game is incredible. Every decision matters, from politics and alliances to marriages and betrayals. It creates situations that feel personal and unpredictable, which makes every playthrough different.

What really makes the game fun is the role-playing aspect. You’re not just controlling a nation—you’re controlling characters with their own traits, goals, and flaws. That makes the experience feel more alive than most strategy games.

The learning curve can be a bit steep at first, but once you understand the systems, it becomes very rewarding. There’s always something new happening, and the game does a great job of keeping you engaged over long play sessions.

Overall, Crusader Kings 3 is a fantastic strategy game with endless replay value. It’s perfect for players who enjoy deep systems and emergent storytelling. 

Gameplay: 9/10 Great | Overall: 9/10 Great

claims.claim: Reviewers point out that setting certain game rules, such as accepting same-sex marriage, disables achievements unless modified.

citations.review_text: I have spent so many hours on this game over the years. Would I do it again? Probably not. The roleplay is fun and immersive for a while, but then gets repetitive unless you add in mods. Also, this game is terrible for charging for add-ons. Why cant games just release in one big chunk nowadays like Cyberpunk or BG3? I'm even ok with one or two quality and substantial expansions, but its just a constant trickle of $4.99 or $15.99 expansion packs that really don't add a lot to the overall game. I am tired of being nickel and dimed for a complete game experience. Oh, and one petty thing that makes me rate them badly, they turn off achievements if you set same-sex marriage as accepted in the game as well. Give us a break.

I really, really wanted to like this game. Give it a fair shot. Experience what it has to offer. But, after spending 200 hours on giving it a chance, I don't think I've had a single consistently positive experience. This is a game for masochists who like to pretend their content has a noteworthy level of historical accuracy. Everything about the game seems designed to make you suffer, from the combat mechanics being obtuse enough that not even the in-game "imminent battle" predictions know what's going on reliably, to the cultural features not actually telling you any real details about what they do, to the absurd difficulty of just becoming a feudal government, to the fact that half the game's rules options disable achievements unless you circumvent that pain point with a mod.... pick literally any goal. The game will always, within the span of around three or four generations, find a way to make you feel bad about having tried to do whatever it is you started it up for.

I bought this game for $17 on sale and I still feel kind of ripped off. Also, there's a ton of functionality that just... isn't there, unless you shell out over $200 for all the 'content' DLCs. Do not, under any circumstances, buy any of this nonsense at full price.

claims.claim: Reviewers note that the game features a subscription option for accessing downloadable content.

citations.review_text: Avoid all Paradox games at all costs. A once proud and amazing studio is gone, and in its place are broken games, and endless over priced DLC products that only change the game incrementally. They update policy gives you a third of new DLC's, but without any way of actually manipulating the new mechanics unless you pay for the whole thing. You might say, 'then don't download the updates', to which I will point out that all bug fixes are handled in these updates, and updates are tied to mods, so if you don't update the game nothing gets fixed and the mods break. Either way, you update the game and the publisher makes the game worse, you don't update and the game slowly loses functionality, your choice.

If you're looking for a well-balanced medieval strategy game where you have to secure both your dynasty and your kingdom, go play Medieval II: Total War. You will not find that game here. 

This game, first and foremost, is a story generator. The goal of Crusader Kings 3 is to make memorable experiences through emergent gameplay and player meddling. The game is designed around playing different characters, dynasties and kingdoms to create whatever scenario you can imagine. If you try to play it as a serious strategy game, you will likely become disappointed by how easy it is, only to become frustrated when you're suddenly invaded by 100k army. The poor balance sucks for a serious strategy experience, but it is excellent when you're able to change characters mid-game. 

Another major problem is the DLC. I would not suggest getting this game without dlc. There is a monthly subscription to get all the dlc but I can understand some people's apprehensions to this.  My strongest recommendation is to get tours and tournaments, roads to power, and all under heaven before you play the game. 

Honestly, I would suggest this game to people who have played the likes of Worldbox or Dwarf Fortress. CK3 shines when you aren't trying to beat the game

Good game but paradox doesnt want regular customers, they only want paypigs and whales since literally no one else is willing to spend €30 for a couple of buttons and modifiers. Take a break for a while and you now have to spend the price of a triple A game just to catch up. Or you can spend €10 a month to own nothing (and be happy!). But you don't understand, they need to charge you a small fortune so that they can continue providing free updated to the poor and huddled masses ;(((((((((((((( even though they routinely get blown out of the water by modders who make things for free but oh well.
